title: Opinion: Your Standing Desk Did Not Fix Your Life, and I Would Know
subtitle: Eleven months in, a full accounting of everything a $600 motorized desk did and did not change about the author's personality, focus, and general disposition.
excerpt: The desk goes up. The desk goes down. You remain, disappointingly, yourself.
author: By Julian Vance
heroHTML:
DESK HEIGHT: 104CM

LIFE STATUS: UNCHANGED

OPINION
bodyHTML:
I want to speak to every person who has told me, unprompted, that switching to a standing desk "changed everything." It did not change everything. I have been standing at mine for eleven months. My posture is marginally better. Everything else about my life is exactly, precisely the same.

This is not a piece about ergonomics. Stand if you like standing. My complaint is narrower and, I think, more important: the standing desk has been marketed to an entire generation of tech workers as a kind of personal transformation device, a $600 intervention that will fix focus, mood, career trajectory, and possibly your relationship with your father, when in fact it is a desk that goes up and down.

"I bought the desk in January telling myself it was the first step toward a completely rebuilt daily routine. It is now September. I use it to stand while doom-scrolling, same as I used to sit while doom-scrolling."
— The author, on the author

Somewhere along the way, "I got a standing desk" became shorthand for "I am taking my life seriously now," in the same category as buying a nice water bottle or downloading a habit tracker you will use for six days. None of these purchases are bad. None of them are the intervention they're sold as.

I am not asking anyone to sit back down. I am asking that we stop describing furniture height as a personality upgrade. The desk goes up. The desk goes down. You remain, disappointingly, yourself.
